The name Tarsicius carries the meaning “Tarsus, Roman nobleman” and is chosen by families in Christian traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Biblical tradition and is also used in English, Hebrew, Greek. data.cultural_impact: The name Tarsicius holds a significant cultural impact in the Catholic Church, particularly in the Roman Catholic tradition. Tarsicius is venerated as a saint, and his story is often portrayed in art and literature. He is typically depicted as a young man or boy carrying a priest over his shoulders while being pursued by soldiers. This image of selfless protection and courage has resonated throughout history and continues to inspire and be a source of pride for those with the name Tarsicius.
data.spiritual_significance: From a spiritual perspective, Tarsicius' story serves as a powerful reminder of the importance of faith and the courage to stand up for it, even in the face of danger. It also illustrates the selfless sacrifice and devotion that Christians are called to demonstrate. Tarsicius' name is a testament to the enduring power and reach of the Christian faith, and a reminder of the courage and determination that is required to live it out in a faith-filled manner.
data.spiritual_symbolism: Tarsicius is believed to be the name of a Roman deacon martyred during the persecutions of Emperor Nero. He is remembered for his courage in carrying the sacred vessels to the catacombs during the persecution, and was martyred when he was found out. Tarsicius represents the strength and faith of the early Christian community in the face of persecution and adversity.

historical_references.reference: Tarsicius was a deacon and martyr from Rome, venerated as a saint in the Catholic Church. He is traditionally believed to have been martyred during the persecutions of Emperor Nero in the 1st century AD. According to legend, Tarsicius refused to surrender the consecrated eucharist to the Roman soldiers during Nero's persecutions, and was subsequently killed.

Another legend tells that Tarsicius, while serving as a deacon under the Bishop Eleutherius of Fiesole, was sent with the eucharist to the sick. He was intercepted by the soldiers of the Emperor Maximian, who demanded that he surrender it. Tarsicius refused, and was beaten and killed. After his death, his body was buried in the church in Fiesole, where he is now venerated as a saint.
